areas.label: Leases
areas.blurb: The invariant this system exists to protect
areas.title: Leases and the failure this system exists to prevent
areas.summary: A lease ends when the job says so, when a deadline the user wrote down elapses, or when a human takes it back. Nothing else — not a socket error, not a probe timeout, not a device going offline, not a pod dying. The invariant is enforced in four independent places: a CHECK constraint with no word for connectivity, four guard-trigger rules, a Postgres role with SELECT revoked on the health table, and a one-way package dependency with a test behind it. All fifteen assertions in test/assertions.sql pass against a database migrated from this tree, and every example below was run against the live farm or a scratch database migrated from it. What is NOT enforced is named in Gaps: there is no host-side fence proxy, the max_runtime sweep ignores protected and ignores the reaper's kill switch, and the witness loop is written and tested end to end while nothing on a placement path starts it. Four things this page used to name here are closed, and are recorded with what closed them rather than deleted: authentication can be turned on, farm.events is a ledger of endings written by a trigger in the same transaction as the ending, the max_runtime sweep fences and rearms like every other ending, and farm_lease_suspect is armed at zero on a fresh process.

areas.label: Jobs
areas.blurb: The step vocabulary, execution, checkpoint and resume
areas.title: Jobs: the step vocabulary, execution, checkpoint and resume
areas.summary: A job is an ordered list of steps drawn from a closed ten-kind vocabulary the database owns (farm.step_kinds), run against one leased device by internal/runner. Only three things end a step badly: its own timeout, an error nothing can retry, or the job's max_runtime. A dropped ADB socket is none of those — it is retried inside the lease with no attempt cap, bounded only by a deadline the job's author wrote down. Long work belongs in a shell_detached step, because that is the only kind whose result lives on the device instead of in a socket the control plane happens to be holding.

areas.label: Devices
areas.title: Devices: enrollment, identity, topology and health
areas.summary: A device in this farm is identified by where it is plugged in, not by what it calls itself: OEM serials collide, and this rack has a clone pair (0123456789ABCDEF at usb:3-1.1 and usb:3-1.2) to prove it. Identity is observed, then resolved against a four-rung ladder — branded uid, hardware fingerprint, serial-plus-slot, adopt — and then branded back onto the phone so the strongest rung exists next time. Health is a third clock kept strictly apart from leases: the watchdog writes one table, has no privilege on farm.leases at all, and a device going offline never takes it away from a running job. Read the Gaps before you rely on any of the enrollment or topology machinery. The fingerprint rung executes now — it called min(uuid), an aggregate PostgreSQL does not have, and migration 00005 rewrote it to count first and fetch second — but the serial rung still cannot return ambiguous, and neither enrollment nor topology discovery runs anywhere except the farmd node role on Linux.

areas.label: Recovery
areas.blurb: The ladder, blast radius, quarantine and bulk
areas.title: Recovery, quarantine, blast radius and bulk operations
areas.summary: The recovery ladder repairs devices underneath live leases. It reads farm.leases in exactly one function, only to decide whether it is allowed to act, and no code path in internal/recovery writes one. Every rung declares a blast radius and the minimum disruption_policy a live lease in that radius must carry; a rung that would reach a lease forbidding it is refused outright, recorded in farm.recovery_attempts.refusal, and the device stays broken until the work on it ends. All three of the things that used to cost you a night are fixed: host drain is enforced by the allocator; tiers 3 and 4 have a client, a column to find a host agent through, and a refusal that survives into farm.recovery_attempts.refusal instead of being flattened to failed; and closing a quarantine now finishes where the operator called it. POST /api/v1/quarantines/{id}/close writes farm.device_runtime.health and farm.devices.admin_state in the SAME transaction as closed_at and answers with devices_released and devices_reenabled, so a farm running no recovery role still gets its devices back. The ladder's own metrics reach /metrics too: the name collision that made recovery.Collectors() unregisterable is gone, and cmd/farmd/roles.go registers every package's group.

areas.label: Interfaces
areas.blurb: HTTP API, the ctl CLI and artifacts
areas.title: The API, the CLI and artifacts
areas.summary: Forty-one routes hang off one net/http pattern mux; the role each needs is chosen at registration in internal/api/router.go, not inside the handler, so no endpoint can exist without a level. Every non-2xx body is the same envelope, and two of its codes are load-bearing: 410 fenced means the lease is gone and the job must abort, 503 transient means the database did not answer and the lease is untouched — conflating them is STF #663. That authorisation can be turned on now: cmd/farmd/roles.go asks api.AuthenticatorFor, which reads FARM_API_TOKENS and refuses to start an exposed listener with no credentials rather than booting open. What is still only a promise is the fence — the API bumps it on a revoke and cooperating clients honour it, but the proxy that would enforce it at the ADB socket is not written, and the revoke response says otherwise in so many words.

areas.label: Operating
areas.title: Running it: roles, configuration, deployment, and what is not built
areas.summary: farmd is one static binary with thirteen subcommands; every role is a subcommand so a reaper can never run a different commit than the scheduler it races with. This page is the authoritative configuration reference — 28 variables in internal/config plus 7 read elsewhere, four of which are validated at boot and then ignored — and the honest inventory of what is not wired. Four entries that used to head that inventory are closed: authentication is chosen by configuration, `farmd node` starts, the recovery ladder has a client for the host agent, and a Helm chart ships. What remains is the metrics gap, and it is worse than it used to read: /metrics carries no package's own series at all, because cmd/farmd/roles.go calls obs.RegisterAll with no collector groups and the tree's single Collectors() call site sits in a branch farmd never takes. The one thing to carry away: SIGTERM drains work and releases nothing, deliberately.

areas.label: Requirements
areas.blurb: Every requirement, its origin, and whether it holds — re-verified against HEAD
areas.summary:
One hundred and one requirements — functional and non-functional — mined from nine commits, the 88 gap entries on the six pages beside this one, the migrations that are the real contract, and three external findings that never touched the code. Each carries an origin, a status verified against this tree rather than copied from the commit that claimed it, and the command that decided it.

Sixty-nine rows are `met` outright and eight more are `met` in one dimension and open in another. Twenty-one remain genuinely open, and the honest headline is what separates them: six need a rack. `farmd node` reads `/sys` and stops at USB discovery anywhere but Linux, so USB reset, VBUS power switching and the fence proxy's host half are written, tested against `fstest.MapFS` and `test/fakeadb`, and have never met a phone. Nine more are reporting — an operator can find out what happened, sometimes only through `psql`. Six are named and deliberately not done.

Read it for three things the area pages cannot show. The couplings: `OPS-04` was one guard in `runNode` blocking four separate requirements, which is why it led the list and why four rows moved with it. The wrong remedies — a surface that tells an operator something is protected when it is not is worse than a documented absence, and this register found four of them. And the requirements with no code at all: managed device clouds are excluded by four suppliers' contracts, so owning the hardware is the path.
areas.title: Every requirement raised for this system, where it came from, and whether it holds
